question: Contoso Health's ingestion API accepts clinical PDFs and hands each one to a Python worker that chunks the document, calls Azure OpenAI for embeddings, and writes vectors to a search index. Uploads burst to 4,000 documents in about three minutes while the worker pool sustains roughly 120 documents per minute, and no document may be lost if every worker instance is recycled mid-batch. Which messaging design fits these requirements?
options: Publish one message per document to an Azure Service Bus queue and have workers receive in peek-lock mode, completing each message only after the vectors are committed
Publish one event per document to an Azure Event Grid custom topic and register the worker's HTTP endpoint as a webhook subscriber
Have the ingestion API call the worker's HTTP endpoint directly and retry in-process when the worker returns a 503 during the burst
Write each document's metadata to a database table and have workers poll that table every second for rows whose status column is still pending
optionExplanations: Correct. This is a durable back-end command, not a notification: the work must survive a burst that exceeds worker throughput and survive instance recycles. A Service Bus queue absorbs the 4,000-message spike as a backlog the workers drain at their own rate, and peek-lock means a message that was being processed when an instance died is unlocked and redelivered rather than lost.

Event Grid is a reactive notification service for state changes, not a work buffer you drain at your own pace — it pushes to subscribers and expects a fast acknowledgement. During a 4,000-document burst the worker endpoint would be pushed far past its 120-per-minute capacity, and slow or failed handlers rely on Event Grid retries rather than a backlog you control.

Direct HTTP calls make the producer's availability depend on the consumer's: there is no buffer, so the burst overwhelms the workers immediately, and in-process retry state is lost the moment the API instance restarts. Coupling a bursty producer to a slower consumer without a broker is the exact failure this queue-based design exists to prevent.

A polled status table can be made durable, but it reimplements a broker badly: you must hand-roll leasing, visibility timeouts, retry counts, and poison-message handling, and one-second polling across many workers creates contention on the same rows. Service Bus already provides locking, delivery counts, and dead-lettering as managed behavior.
principle: durable back-end commands belong on a queue, not on a notification bus
relatedConcept: Choosing between Service Bus and Event Grid starts with asking whether the payload is a command someone must eventually execute or a notification that something happened.
overallExplanation: Use a Service Bus queue with peek-lock when work items are durable commands that must survive bursts and instance restarts. Event Grid is for reactive state-change notification; a queue is for buffered, at-least-once execution of back-end operations.

question: A retail platform publishes a ProductUpdated message for every catalog change. Three independent back-end services must each act on every message: an embedding refresher, a price-index rebuilder, and an audit archiver. Today all three read from one Service Bus queue, and each message is processed by whichever service receives it first, so the other two never see it. What is the correct fix?
options: Replace the queue with a Service Bus topic and give each service its own subscription so all three receive an independent copy of every message
Keep the single queue but have each service peek messages instead of receiving them, so a message stays available to the other two services
Keep the single queue and enable sessions, assigning each service a distinct session id so each one gets its own stream of messages
Keep the single queue and have the publisher send three copies of every message, one tagged for each consuming service
optionExplanations: Correct. A queue is a competing-consumers construct: one message goes to exactly one receiver. A topic with three subscriptions gives each service a durable, independently tracked copy, with its own delivery count, its own dead-letter queue, and its own backlog — which is precisely the durable publish-subscribe shape this scenario needs.

Peeking returns messages without locking them, so nothing is ever removed and the same messages are read forever. Peek is a diagnostic and browsing operation, not a delivery mode: it gives you no lock, no completion, and no way to track which service has finished which message.

Sessions group related messages so they are handled in order by a single consumer; the session id comes from the producer's partitioning intent, not from consumer identity. Assigning a session per service would just split the single stream three ways — each message still lands in only one session and therefore reaches only one service.

Publisher-side fan-out works only until the fourth consumer appears, and it puts routing knowledge in the producer: adding, removing, or filtering a consumer becomes a code change and a redeploy. Topics move that routing into the broker, where a new subscription is a configuration change with no producer impact.
principle: queues are competing consumers, topics and subscriptions are durable pub/sub
relatedConcept: Service Bus topics add a routing layer on top of queue semantics: each subscription behaves like its own queue with its own locks, delivery counts, and dead-letter queue.
overallExplanation: When several independent services each need every message, use a Service Bus topic with one subscription per service. A single queue distributes each message to exactly one competing consumer, which is why two of the three services never see it.

question: A conversational-AI back end persists each user turn as a message that a worker applies to a per-conversation summary document. With eight concurrent workers, turns from the same conversation are sometimes applied out of order, producing summaries that mention a reply before the question that prompted it. Throughput across conversations must stay parallel. What should the team change?
options: Enable sessions on the queue and set session_id to the conversation id so all turns for one conversation are processed in order by a single receiver
Reduce the consumer pool to a single worker instance so that messages are always processed strictly in the order they were enqueued
Set a longer lock duration on the queue so each worker holds its message long enough for earlier messages to be applied first
Enable duplicate detection on the queue so that repeated turns from the same conversation are collapsed into a single ordered message
optionExplanations: Correct. Session-enabled queues bind all messages sharing a session_id to one receiver at a time and deliver them in order within that session. Using the conversation id as the session id preserves per-conversation ordering while different sessions are still processed concurrently by different workers, so overall throughput is unaffected.

A single consumer does restore global ordering, but it throws away all cross-conversation parallelism and makes one slow turn block every other user's conversation. The requirement is ordering within a conversation, not ordering across the whole queue, and sessions give exactly that narrower guarantee.

Lock duration controls how long a receiver may hold a message before it becomes visible again; it says nothing about the relative order in which independent receivers pick messages up. Lengthening it would only delay redelivery of stalled messages while the interleaving that caused the bug continues unchanged.

Duplicate detection suppresses messages that repeat the same MessageId inside a time window. These turns are distinct messages, not duplicates, so nothing would be filtered and the ordering problem would remain exactly as it is.
principle: sessions give ordered, single-receiver processing per partition key
relatedConcept: Service Bus guarantees FIFO only within a session, which is how you get per-entity ordering without giving up parallelism across entities.
overallExplanation: Use session-enabled queues with the conversation id as session_id to guarantee in-order processing per conversation while keeping different conversations parallel. Ordering in Service Bus is a per-session guarantee, not a queue-wide one.

question: A summarization worker receives from a Service Bus queue whose lock duration is the maximum five minutes. Long documents take six to nine minutes because of a chained Azure OpenAI call. Telemetry shows those documents being summarized two or three times, and complete_message() then fails with a lock-lost error. The team cannot shorten the model call. What is the correct remedy?
options: Wrap the receiver in an AutoLockRenewer (or call renew_message_lock periodically) so the lock is extended for the duration of the long-running call
Raise the queue's lock duration to fifteen minutes so it comfortably exceeds the worst-case processing time
Switch the receiver to receive-and-delete mode so the message is removed immediately and cannot be redelivered
Increase MaxDeliveryCount so the extra deliveries no longer push the message toward the dead-letter queue
optionExplanations: Correct. Five minutes is the hard ceiling for lock duration, so the only supported way to hold a message longer is to renew the lock while you work. AutoLockRenewer renews in the background up to a configured maximum, which keeps the message invisible to other receivers for the whole nine-minute call and lets complete_message() succeed.

Service Bus caps lock duration at five minutes, so this value cannot be configured — the attempt fails rather than fixing anything. The design assumption is that longer work is covered by lock renewal, not by an ever-larger lock window.

Receive-and-delete does stop redelivery, but it does so by deleting the message before processing: if the worker crashes during the nine-minute call the document is silently lost with no retry. That trades a duplicate-processing bug for a data-loss bug, which is a worse outcome for an ingestion pipeline.

Raising MaxDeliveryCount only changes how many redeliveries occur before dead-lettering. The message would still be picked up repeatedly by other receivers and still cost duplicate model calls; the root cause is an expired lock, not an exhausted delivery budget.
principle: renew the lock when work outlives it; never stretch the lock beyond its ceiling
relatedConcept: Peek-lock makes a message invisible for the lock duration; if processing can exceed that window, lock renewal is the mechanism that keeps ownership.
overallExplanation: Lock duration maxes out at five minutes, so long AI calls must renew the lock — AutoLockRenewer or explicit renew_message_lock. Duplicate processing plus lock-lost errors on completion is the signature of work outliving its lock.

question: An overnight enrichment queue has accumulated 812 messages in its dead-letter queue. Sampling shows two causes: about 90 percent were malformed payloads that raise a parse error on every delivery until MaxDeliveryCount was exhausted, and the rest expired while a downstream service was offline. The team needs a supportable dead-letter strategy. Which two actions are appropriate? (Choose two.)
options: Build a triage consumer that receives from the queue's dead-letter sub-queue and reads DeadLetterReason and DeadLetterErrorDescription to classify each message
Explicitly dead-letter a message with a reason as soon as the payload fails schema validation, instead of letting it burn through ten deliveries first
Raise MaxDeliveryCount on the queue to 200 so malformed messages have more chances to succeed before being dead-lettered
Disable dead-lettering on the queue so that failing messages stay in the active queue and are retried indefinitely
optionExplanations: Correct. The dead-letter queue is a real sub-queue you read with an ordinary receiver, and Service Bus stamps DeadLetterReason and DeadLetterErrorDescription on each message. A triage consumer that reads those properties can separate poison payloads that need a code or data fix from transient failures that can simply be resubmitted.

Correct. A payload that cannot be parsed will never succeed, so letting it consume the full delivery budget wastes ten receives, ten model-adjacent code paths, and roughly ten times the latency before it lands where it belongs. Calling dead_letter_message with an explicit reason moves a known-unrecoverable message aside immediately and records why.

This scales the wrong dimension: a deterministic parse failure fails identically on delivery 200 as on delivery 1, so a higher delivery count only multiplies wasted work and delays discovery. Delivery count exists to absorb transient faults, not to grind against permanently invalid data.

Turning dead-lettering off removes the quarantine that keeps poison messages from blocking the pipeline: they return to the active queue forever, consuming receiver capacity and hiding the failure signal. The dead-letter queue is the mechanism that makes bad messages visible instead of endlessly recycled.
principle: dead-letter deliberately, then triage on the reason the broker recorded
relatedConcept: Dead-lettering is the poison-message boundary: it separates messages that can never succeed from a healthy pipeline, and records why so a human or a repair job can act.
overallExplanation: Treat the dead-letter sub-queue as a first-class endpoint — receive from it and classify on DeadLetterReason — and dead-letter known-invalid payloads immediately rather than exhausting MaxDeliveryCount. Raising delivery counts or disabling dead-lettering only hides poison messages.

question: A billing-adjacent worker consumes a Service Bus queue and, for each message, calls Azure OpenAI and appends a usage row. During a deployment that recycled pods mid-processing, several messages were redelivered and the usage table gained duplicate rows for the same source document. The team wants correctness without giving up the queue's durability. What is the right change?
options: Derive an idempotency key from the business payload, carry it on the message, and make the usage write conditional on that key so a replay is a no-op
Switch the receiver to receive-and-delete so a redelivery can never happen after a pod is recycled
Enable duplicate detection on the queue, which will prevent the consumer from processing the same message twice
Reduce MaxDeliveryCount to 1 so a message that fails once is dead-lettered instead of being redelivered
optionExplanations: Correct. Service Bus is an at-least-once system: a crash after the side effect but before completion necessarily produces a redelivery. The only place that can be fixed is the consumer, by making the effect idempotent — a stable business key plus a conditional or upsert write means the second application changes nothing.

Receive-and-delete removes the message before the work runs, so a pod recycled mid-processing loses the document entirely. It eliminates duplicates by introducing silent data loss, which is unacceptable for a pipeline whose output feeds billing.

Duplicate detection is a producer-side feature: it discards messages whose MessageId repeats within the detection window at send time. It does nothing about redelivery of an already-accepted message caused by an expired lock or a crashed consumer, which is what happened here.

MaxDeliveryCount of 1 converts every transient blip — a throttled model call, a brief network fault, a pod recycle — into an immediate dead-letter, so the pipeline sheds legitimate work. It also does not eliminate duplicates, because the duplicate here came from the first delivery's partially applied side effect.
principle: at-least-once delivery makes idempotency the consumer's job
relatedConcept: Brokers guarantee that a message is delivered at least once, never exactly once, so any consumer with side effects needs a business key that makes reapplication harmless.
overallExplanation: At-least-once delivery means redelivery is normal, so the consumer must be idempotent via a business or idempotency key and a conditional write. Duplicate detection is producer-side, and receive-and-delete trades duplicates for data loss.

question: An ingestion pipeline runs producer to Service Bus queue to worker, where each worker chunks a document, calls an embedding model, then writes to a vector store. Over four hours the queue's active message count climbs from 40 to 61,000 while consumer CPU sits at 22 percent and the vector-store write span averages 2.9 seconds against 180 milliseconds for embedding. What does the backlog tell you?
options: The vector-store write is the slowest stage and is setting end-to-end throughput, so the backlog will keep growing until that stage is made faster or more parallel
The producers are emitting messages faster than the broker can accept them, so the queue itself is the bottleneck and needs a higher tier
The workers are CPU-starved, and scaling the consumer pool out will drain the backlog regardless of where time is spent
The backlog is a normal buffering artifact of an asynchronous pipeline and needs no action as long as no messages are dead-lettered
optionExplanations: Correct. A monotonically growing backlog means arrival rate exceeds completion rate, and completion rate is governed by the slowest stage in the consumer path. With writes at 2.9 seconds against 180 milliseconds for embedding, roughly 94 percent of each message's service time is the vector-store write, so that stage is the constraint to widen.

The queue accepted every message — that is why the backlog exists and keeps growing. A broker that could not keep up would surface throttling or send failures on the producer side, not a cleanly accumulating count of successfully enqueued messages.

Twenty-two percent CPU is direct evidence the workers are not compute-bound; they are blocked waiting on a downstream dependency. Adding instances that all wait on the same saturated vector store usually increases contention and error rates rather than throughput.

Buffering is normal, but a backlog that rises steadily for four hours with no plateau is not buffering — it is a throughput deficit, and latency for the newest message grows without bound. Dead-lettering is a separate signal and its absence does not make an unbounded backlog healthy.
principle: a growing queue depth points at the slowest downstream stage
relatedConcept: Queue depth is the cheapest throughput telemetry in a message-driven system: it rises exactly when consumption cannot match arrival, and the span breakdown says which stage is responsible.
overallExplanation: A steadily growing backlog with idle consumer CPU means the constraint is downstream, and the span breakdown identifies it — here the 2.9-second vector-store write. Fix or parallelize the slowest stage; scaling consumers that are already blocked does not add throughput.

question: A storage account raises Blob Created events for every upload across many containers. A reindexing function should run only for blobs written under the documents/incoming/ prefix and only when the event data's contentType is application/pdf. Today the function receives every blob event and discards about 95 percent of them in code. What is the best change?
options: Configure the event subscription with a subject filter for the documents/incoming/ prefix plus an advanced filter on data.contentType, so Event Grid delivers only matching events
Keep the broad subscription and move the discard logic to the top of the handler so the function returns earlier on non-matching events
Create a separate storage account for PDF uploads so that the existing subscription naturally receives only relevant events
Subscribe to the events with a Service Bus topic in between and write a SQL rule on the subscription that inspects the blob path
optionExplanations: Correct. Event Grid filters at the subscription, so non-matching events are never delivered and never billed as handler executions. Subject filtering handles the path prefix and advanced filters evaluate fields inside the event payload such as data.contentType, which together express exactly the 5 percent the function cares about.

Returning early still pays for delivery, a function invocation, cold-start risk, and log volume for every one of the discarded events. It optimizes the handler's inner loop while leaving the real waste — twenty times more invocations than necessary — completely in place.

Restructuring storage to encode routing is a heavy, disruptive answer to a filtering problem, and it breaks down the moment a second routing dimension such as content type or tenant appears. Subscription filters express the same intent as configuration, without moving any data.

Interposing a Service Bus topic adds a hop, a second broker, and a second set of failure modes purely to run a rule that Event Grid can already evaluate itself. It is the right pattern when you also need durable buffering or competing consumers, not when the requirement is simply to stop delivering irrelevant events.
principle: filter at the subscription so irrelevant events are never delivered
relatedConcept: Event Grid subscription filters — subject prefix and suffix plus advanced filters over event fields — push routing decisions into the broker instead of the handler.
overallExplanation: Express routing as Event Grid subscription filters: subject prefix for the path and an advanced filter on data.contentType. Filtering in handler code still pays the delivery, invocation, and logging cost for every event you throw away.

question: A SaaS team wants other teams to react to its own domain milestones — ModelPromoted, IndexRebuilt, EvaluationCompleted — without the publisher knowing who consumes them. Consumers must be able to subscribe to one event type without receiving the others, and the publisher wants a standards-based envelope. What should the team build?
options: Publish custom events to an Event Grid custom topic using the CloudEvents schema, letting each consumer create a subscription filtered on eventType
Publish the milestones to a single Service Bus queue and let each consuming team receive from it and ignore the types it does not care about
Expose a REST endpoint that consumers poll every minute for new milestones, returning any that occurred since the caller's last cursor
Write the milestones to a shared blob container and let each consuming team enumerate new blobs on a schedule
optionExplanations: Correct. A custom topic is exactly the publisher-owned endpoint for domain events, and Event Grid supports the CloudEvents v1.0 schema as a standard envelope. Each consumer then owns its own subscription with an eventType filter, so adding or removing a consumer never touches publisher code — the defining property of reactive, decoupled notification.

A single queue is competing consumers: the first team to receive a milestone takes it away from the others, so this design silently starves every consumer but one. It also forces each team to filter in code and to coordinate on a shared receiver, which is the coupling the team is trying to eliminate.

Polling inverts the model the team asked for: consumers must know the publisher's endpoint, manage cursors, and choose a polling interval that trades latency against wasted requests. It also puts read load on the publisher proportional to the number of consumers rather than to the number of events.

A shared blob container turns an eventing problem into a filesystem-enumeration problem, with no per-consumer filtering, no delivery guarantees, no retries, and no dead-lettering. Consumers would each reimplement change detection and de-duplication over blob listings.
principle: custom topics plus per-consumer subscriptions decouple publishers from subscribers
relatedConcept: Event Grid custom topics let an application emit its own domain events in the CloudEvents schema, and subscriptions determine who receives which of them.
overallExplanation: Publish domain milestones as custom events to an Event Grid custom topic in the CloudEvents schema, and let each consumer own an eventType-filtered subscription. Queues give competing consumers, and polling reintroduces the coupling events exist to remove.

question: An Event Grid subscription delivers to a webhook that was down for a two-hour maintenance window. Afterwards the team finds some events were delivered late, but a portion never arrived at all and no record of them exists anywhere. They need to guarantee that undeliverable events are recoverable in future outages. Which two configuration changes address this? (Choose two.)
options: Configure a dead-letter destination on the event subscription so events that exhaust retries are written to a storage container
Raise the subscription's event time-to-live so events remain retryable for longer than a planned maintenance window
Increase the webhook's HTTP timeout so Event Grid waits longer for a response before counting a delivery as failed
Switch the subscription's delivery schema to CloudEvents so that failed deliveries are automatically preserved by Event Grid
optionExplanations: Correct. Without a dead-letter destination, an event that exhausts its retry policy is simply dropped — which is exactly why some events left no trace. Pointing the subscription at a blob container means exhausted events land somewhere durable, with delivery metadata, so they can be inspected and replayed after the outage.

Correct. Event Grid retries until either the maximum delivery attempts or the event time-to-live is reached, whichever comes first, and the default TTL is 24 hours. Sizing the TTL against the longest outage the team expects to absorb is what keeps events retryable rather than expired during a maintenance window.

The delivery timeout governs how long Event Grid waits for a single response from a handler that is answering slowly. During this incident the endpoint was down, so requests failed immediately — a longer wait per attempt changes nothing about whether the event survives two hours of unavailability.

The delivery schema controls the envelope format of the event payload — CloudEvents versus the Event Grid schema — and has no bearing on retention or retry behavior. Preservation of undeliverable events comes from the dead-letter destination, not from the serialization format.
principle: retries need both a time budget and a place for events that exhaust it
relatedConcept: Event Grid retry policy is bounded by maximum delivery attempts and event time-to-live; anything that exhausts both is discarded unless a dead-letter destination is configured.
overallExplanation: Give the subscription a dead-letter destination so exhausted events land in durable storage, and size the event TTL against realistic outage windows. Delivery timeouts and schema choice do not affect whether an undeliverable event is retained.

question: A worker calls a partner API that returns 503 with a Retry-After of about 90 seconds during the partner's nightly window. Today the worker abandons the message on failure, so Service Bus redelivers it within milliseconds; the message churns through its whole delivery budget in under a second and dead-letters, even though it would have succeeded a couple of minutes later. What is the best fix?
options: On a transient failure, complete the message and re-send a copy with scheduled_enqueue_time_utc set past the retry window, carrying an attempt counter in the application properties
Keep abandoning the message but raise MaxDeliveryCount to 500 so the churn eventually outlasts the partner's maintenance window
Have the worker sleep for 90 seconds inside the message handler and retry the partner call in place before completing the message
Set the queue's lock duration to 90 seconds so an abandoned message cannot be redelivered until the partner has recovered
optionExplanations: Correct. Abandon makes a message immediately visible again, which is why the delivery budget evaporates in under a second. Scheduling a fresh copy for a future enqueue time turns redelivery into a real backoff: the message leaves the active queue, stops consuming receiver capacity, and reappears after the partner window, with the attempt counter carrying the retry state.

A larger delivery budget still gets consumed at the same millisecond cadence, so this mostly converts a fast failure into a burst of hundreds of pointless receives and partner calls. It treats the symptom — dead-lettering — while leaving the actual defect, retry with no delay, untouched.

Sleeping inside the handler holds the message lock and an entire concurrency slot idle for 90 seconds, so a queue of such messages stalls the whole consumer pool. It also risks exceeding the lock without renewal, which reintroduces duplicate processing on top of the throughput loss.

Lock duration bounds how long a receiver may hold a message; abandon explicitly releases the lock early, so the lock setting has no effect on how quickly an abandoned message returns. The delay has to be expressed on the message's enqueue time, not on the lock.
principle: backoff must delay the message, not just re-deliver it faster
relatedConcept: Scheduled messages let a consumer implement real backoff by pushing a retry into the future instead of spinning through the delivery count immediately.
overallExplanation: Abandon returns a message instantly, so it is not backoff. Re-send with scheduled_enqueue_time_utc beyond the retry window and track attempts on the message, which frees consumer capacity and preserves the delivery budget for genuine failures.

question: A team benchmarking a Service Bus consumer sets prefetch_count to 500 and max_wait_time low, and each message triggers a model call averaging 25 seconds. Throughput barely improves and lock-lost errors appear on messages the consumer has not started yet. Lock duration is five minutes. What explains the result?
options: Prefetched messages have their locks started at fetch time, so with 25-second processing a batch of 500 cannot be handled before the later messages' locks expire
Prefetch is incompatible with peek-lock mode and silently downgrades the receiver to receive-and-delete, which is why locks appear lost
The lock-lost errors come from prefetch bypassing the broker's delivery count, so messages are dead-lettered before the consumer reaches them
Prefetch only helps when messages exceed 256 KB, so a small-payload workload cannot benefit from it under any configuration
optionExplanations: Correct. Prefetch pulls messages into a client-side buffer and their locks begin ticking the moment they are fetched, not when your code touches them. At 25 seconds each, the consumer is still working on message 12 when message 400's five-minute lock has long expired, so prefetch must be sized to what the consumer can finish inside the lock window.

Prefetch and peek-lock work together — that is precisely why prefetched messages carry locks that can expire. There is no silent downgrade to receive-and-delete; if there were, messages would be deleted on fetch rather than reported as lock-lost.

Delivery count is maintained by the broker and is unaffected by client-side prefetching. Messages whose locks expire become visible again and their delivery count increments normally, so they are redelivered rather than skipped straight to dead-letter.

Prefetch is a latency optimization for high-rate, short-processing workloads and has nothing to do with payload size; the 256 KB figure is the standard-tier message size limit. The relevant variable here is per-message processing time relative to lock duration.
principle: size prefetch to what you can process inside the lock window
relatedConcept: Prefetch trades lock safety for latency: it hides broker round trips, but every buffered message is already holding a lock that is counting down.
overallExplanation: Prefetched messages start their lock clock at fetch time, so a large prefetch plus slow per-message work guarantees lock expiry on the tail of the batch. Prefetch suits short, high-rate processing; long model calls need a small prefetch and lock renewal.

question: A document pipeline on a Standard-tier Service Bus namespace sends the full extracted text of each document as the message body. Most documents are a few kilobytes, but scanned reports reach 900 KB and the send call fails for those. The team wants the smallest change that keeps every document flowing through the same queue. What should they do?
options: Write the extracted text to Blob Storage and send a message containing the blob URI and a content hash, letting the consumer fetch the body on receipt
Split the extracted text across several messages of under 256 KB and have the consumer reassemble them before processing
Compress the extracted text with gzip before sending so that every payload fits within the tier limit
Move the consumer to receive-and-delete mode, which removes the per-message size restriction on the queue
optionExplanations: Correct. This is the claim-check pattern: the large payload goes to storage designed for it, and the message carries only a reference plus enough metadata to validate it. It keeps message sizes small and uniform, keeps broker throughput high, and works for a 900 KB scan or a 90 MB one without touching the queue configuration again.

Manual splitting forces the consumer to buffer partial documents, correlate fragments, handle a missing or out-of-order fragment, and clean up after a partial failure. That is a substantial amount of stateful reassembly logic to avoid one blob write, and it fails outright if a document is large enough to need many fragments.

Compression buys a variable, workload-dependent margin — a scanned report's text may compress well or badly — so the failure returns as soon as a document is slightly larger or less compressible. It also hides the size problem behind a ratio nobody controls, rather than removing the ceiling.

Receive mode is a consumer-side concern and has no relationship to the maximum message size the broker will accept on send. The send would fail identically, and the change would additionally introduce data loss on consumer crashes.
principle: put big payloads in storage and send a claim check
relatedConcept: Broker message-size ceilings (256 KB on Standard, far larger on Premium) push large payloads toward a reference-plus-blob design rather than inline bodies.
overallExplanation: Use the claim-check pattern: store the large payload in Blob Storage and send only a URI plus metadata. Splitting adds stateful reassembly, and compression only postpones the ceiling until a slightly larger document arrives.

domain: Connect to and consume Azure services
